**What you should be able to do after this meeting.** Say what a scraper and an API each are, and when either is the wrong answer. Name your own data source, its access route, its timeline and your plan B — including whether you need IRB approval or a data-use agreement before January.

## Before class

**Reading.** TBD

The opening quiz is on this reading.

## Session A · 2:05–3:15

First, code. Not how to write it — what it is, and why you cannot avoid understanding it. What a language actually is, and why there are several. R grew out of statistics. Python out of general programming. Stata out of applied economics. SQL is not really the same kind of thing at all. Then the argument that matters here. Every serious analysis is code, whether or not you wrote it. A spreadsheet stops being enough at exactly the point your project gets interesting. And code is the only version of an analysis that can be checked, repeated, and handed to somebody else. You will drive it through an assistant. But you cannot check what you cannot read at all. Then the landscape of sources: administrative records, official statistics, firm and platform data, purchased panels. What each costs in money and in months, starting with what Cornell already pays for. Proprietary access and data-use agreements: who signs, how long, and what they forbid you from publishing. Ethics and the IRB in brief, with the detail on the resources page. Then scraping and APIs: what each is, what it can and cannot get you, and what the terms of service and the law actually say.

## Session B · 3:35–4:30

Every session B opens with a ten-minute team check-in: what you did
since last week, what is stuck, and who is doing what next. Written
down, and handed in with that session's work.

A scrape, run live from the front, then broken on purpose. We pull a table off a page. Then we watch every way it fails. The page changes and the code returns nothing. The rate limit bites. Records go missing and nothing tells you. The terms of service say no. And nothing you pulled could be reproduced by anybody next week. Then the same data through a proper API. Then the same data simply downloaded, which is usually faster than either. The lesson is not that scraping is bad. It is the last resort dressed up as the clever one. Then the acquisition clinic on your own project. Which source, exactly. What route. How long. What it costs. What plan B is. Your memo outline — six topic sentences — comes out of that, and it is due before the weekend.

Your team's output is submitted before you leave.

## Due
